content: The provided text is a dense compilation of references, study data, and outcomes related to the use of dolutegravir (DTG) and other antiretroviral therapies (ART) in pregnancy, breastfeeding, and their associated outcomes. 1. The study by Ganapathy et al. (2010) highlights the role of placental membrane transporters in the transfer of xenobiotics, including drugs, across the maternal-fetal interface. This research emphasizes the importance of human models in studying drug disposition during pregnancy. 2. Tomi et al. (2000) investigated the transfer of antiviral drugs from mother to fetus, focusing on the involvement of placental transporters. Their findings underscore the critical role of these transporters in modulating drug exposure to the fetus. 3. Nabekura et al. (2015) examined the effects of antiviral drugs on organic anion transport in human placental BeWo cells. Their results provide insights into how these drugs interact with placental transport mechanisms. 4. Rubinchik-Stern et al. (2018) conducted studies on the adverse effects of valproic acid on the placenta using perfused human placentas. Their findings reveal potential risks associated with valproic acid exposure during pregnancy. 5. The DOLPHIN-1 trial (Waitt et al., 2018) compared dolutegravir (DTG) and efavirenz (EFV) in women initiating ART during late pregnancy. The study assessed viral suppression, safety, and pharmacokinetics, providing critical data for treatment decisions in this population. 6. Stover and Winfrey (2017) analyzed the impact of family planning and other factors on fertility, miscarriage, and stillbirth rates using the Spectrum model. Their work offers valuable insights into reproductive health outcomes. 7. Uthman et al. (2017) performed a systematic review and meta-analysis on the timing of ART initiation and its association with adverse pregnancy outcomes. Their findings highlight the importance of early ART initiation to optimize maternal and fetal health. 8. Zash et al. (2018) presented data from Botswana on neural tube defects and other adverse birth outcomes in HIV-positive women exposed to DTG or EFV during pregnancy. The study provides critical safety data for ART use in pregnancy. 9. The International Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry (2018) reported outcomes from pregnancies exposed to DTG, including live births and birth defects. This registry serves as a key resource for monitoring ART safety in pregnancy. 10. The DOLPHIN-2 trial (Khoo et al., 2018) extended the evaluation of DTG versus EFV in late-presenting pregnant women. The study focused on viral suppression, safety, and pharmacokinetics, with ongoing data collection. 11. The ADVANCE trial (Khoo et al., 2018) compared DTG-based regimens with EFV-based regimens in ART-naïve individuals, including pregnant women. Preliminary data suggest favorable outcomes with DTG, though pregnancy-specific data remain limited. 12. The NAMSL trial (2018) in Cameroon evaluated DTG versus EFV as first-line ART in non-pregnant adults, with follow-up for those who became pregnant. The study provides additional safety and efficacy data for DTG in pregnancy. 13. Grayhack et al. (2018) conducted a retrospective cohort study in the USA, analyzing outcomes in HIV-positive women on DTG during pregnancy. The study assessed maternal viral load, birth outcomes, and infant health. 14. Mulligan et al. (2018) performed a pharmacokinetic study of DTG in pregnant women compared to postpartum women. The findings contribute to understanding DTG dosing and safety during pregnancy. 15. Rahangdale et al. (2016) retrospectively analyzed outcomes in pregnant women starting or adding integrase inhibitors, including DTG, to their ART regimens. The study highlights the effectiveness of integrase inhibitors in achieving viral suppression. 16. Pain et al. (2015) reported a case of a pregnant woman with preterm rupture of membranes who received DTG intensification. The study provides pharmacokinetic data on DTG use in preterm infants. 17. Schalkwijk et al. (2016) conducted an ex vivo placental perfusion study to evaluate DTG transfer across the placenta. The results indicate limited placental passage of DTG at therapeutic concentrations. 18. Kobbe et al. (2016) described a case of an HIV-positive woman on DTG postpartum who breastfed her infant. The study assessed DTG transfer into breast milk and its potential impact on the infant. 19. The ARIA trial (Orrell et al., 2017) compared DTG-based regimens with protease inhibitor-based regimens in non-pregnant women. A small subset of participants became pregnant, and their outcomes were monitored. 20. The EPICC cohort (Thorne et al., 2018) provided data on pregnancy outcomes in HIV-positive women receiving DTG in Europe. The study included live births and birth defect assessments. 21. The NSHPC study (Thorne et al., 2018) in the UK and Ireland reported outcomes in HIV-positive women on DTG during pregnancy. The findings contribute to the growing body of evidence on DTG safety in pregnancy. 22. ViiV Healthcare clinical trial safety reports provide additional data on DTG use during pregnancy, including pharmacokinetics, maternal viral suppression, and infant outcomes.
